title: The Uganda Licence Mo Ibrahim's Clients Would Not Touch
conflicts: Uganda timing: Ibrahim dates the Idi Amin conversation to 1998, but the IFC says Celtel Uganda launched in 1995 as the first cellular operator and Satya Capital says Celtel began with a minority holding in that licence; the story does not date the Uganda stake or claim the free licence he was offered became Celtel's. Marconi price for MSI: Ibrahim says more than (or about) $900 million, Agence Europe (April 2000) reported USD 618 million; no price given. Customers and staff at the 2005 sale differ (HBR 5.2m/5,000 staff in 2004; ITWeb >5m; Satya >6m/3,000 staff); the story uses ITWeb's 'more than five million' and gives no staff figure. Years since Amin left: 'years ago' (HBR), '20 years' (CFR), '15 years' (CNBC); the story says 'long ago'. Ibrahim's two accounts also differ on where the first money came from (consultancy per HBR; MSI sale per CFR, which happened in 2000); the story follows HBR.
notes: Kept distinct from the Strive Masiyiwa/Econet licence-fight edition: this is Ibrahim's 1998 turn from consultant to operator, not a licence dispute. Country set to Uganda because the pivotal conversation and Celtel's starting holding both concern Uganda, though the decision was taken in London and the 1998 licences were in Malawi, Zambia, Sierra Leone and Congo-Brazzaville. The slate's 'starting in Uganda' is only partly right: MSI Cellular also held Indian and Hong Kong interests at first (sold by 2000, per RCR). HBR's line that Celtel declined Guinea and Angola was left out because RCR (2000) listed Guinea among planned networks. Agence Europe loads but does not name Ibrahim or Celtel; it is used only for the Marconi cross-check. The repeat screen flags the Samir Ibrahim (SunCulture) edition as same-founder because of the shared surname; it is a different person, and the edition passes unchanged.
